scope: Odisha events — temple traditions, Eastern Ganga and Suryavamsi successions, Paika rebellion, regional first-person sources. Seeded with the Madala Panji.

events.title: Madala Panji: Jagannath temple chronicles
events.tooltip: Madala Panji compilation, Jagannath temple, Puri, c. 16th c. onward
events.summary: Multi-generational palm-leaf chronicle of the Jagannath temple at Puri — Odia institutional first-person record across four centuries.
events.detail: The Madala Panji is the cumulative chronicle of the Jagannath temple at Puri, kept by hereditary Karana scribes. Tradition traces it to the reign of Anantavarman Chodaganga (12th century); surviving palm-leaf manuscripts mostly date from the 16th century onward, after the Suryavamsi-era institutional consolidation and Akbar's general Mansingh's intervention in temple affairs (1592). Written in Odia, the Panji records royal patronage, festival calendars (Rath Yatra, Snana Purnima), Bhoga offerings, ritual schedules, daily temple administration, and political events affecting Puri — the Mughal-Maratha-British contests for temple control across the 17th–19th centuries. Unlike court chronicles spoken from a king's voice, the Madala Panji is institutional first-person — the temple speaking for itself across ruling dynasties. Modern editing began under Hunter (1872) and has continued through Manmath Nath Das, Krushna Chandra Panigrahi, and others.

date.display: c. 16th century onward (extant manuscripts; tradition older)

sources.label: Madala Panji (ed. Krushna Chandra Panigrahi, Utkal University, 1955)
Hermann Kulke, Kings and Cults: State Formation and Legitimation in India and Southeast Asia (1993), ch. on Jagannath
Anncharlott Eschmann, Hermann Kulke, G.C. Tripathi (eds.), The Cult of Jagannath and the Regional Tradition of Orissa (1978)

events.title: Paika Rebellion under Buxi Jagabandhu
events.tooltip: Paika peasant-warrior rebellion in Khurda, Odisha, 1817–1819
events.summary: Buxi Jagabandhu led the dispossessed Paika militia of Khurda against EIC revenue policy — sacked the Khurda fort, held out for two years.
events.detail: The Paikas were the hereditary peasant-warrior militia of the Khurda kingdom of Odisha, holding rent-free service-tenure land (jagir) in exchange for military service to the Khurda Raja. After the EIC annexation of Odisha (1803), the new revenue settlement converted Paika tenures into ordinary cash-rent holdings, levied salt and currency duties on a population accustomed to in-kind transactions, and dispossessed the Paika commander Buxi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar Mohapatra of his ancestral estate at Killa Rorang (1814). On 29 March 1817, Jagabandhu led the Paikas in revolt — sacked the Khurda fort, killed the EIC tahsildar, attacked salt depots and police stations across the Khurda region. Tribals (Kondhs and Savaras) joined; the revolt spread to Pipili, Cuttack, and Puri. EIC suppression took two years; Jagabandhu surrendered in 1825 under amnesty, died in custody at Cuttack 1829. The rebellion was officially recognised by the Government of India in 2017 as a 'first war of independence' on its bicentenary — politically loaded but extending the textbook 1857 framing back forty years.

sources.label: Prabhat Mukherjee, History of the Khurda Raj (1953)
K.C. Jena, History of the Paika Rebellion (Kalinga Books, 1986)

events.title: Khond (Kandh) Risings
events.summary: Khond tribals rebelled against EIC suppression of meriah and against revenue extraction — Chakra Bisoi and Dandasena led repeated risings, 1837–1856.
events.detail: The Khonds (Kandhs) of the Eastern Ghats hill-forest tracts in present-day Odisha — Phulbani, Kandhamal, Koraput — practised meriah, the ritual sacrifice of purchased human victims to the earth goddess Tari Pennu, into the 19th century. The EIC's Meriah Agency (1845) under Major-General John Campbell suppressed the practice through deployment of a special force, freed an estimated 1,500 meriah victims, and imposed increased revenue assessments on the Khond zamindars during the same operations. The Khonds rose repeatedly: under Chakra Bisoi from 1837 in Ghumsur, joined by Dora Bisoi and Radhakrishna Dandasena; the major risings of 1846 and 1855–56 covered Ghumsur, Kalahandi, Boudh, Daspalla. EIC suppression continued through the 1860s. The hill-area administration that emerged from the Meriah Agency persisted as the Agency tract system through colonial rule and the early independence period — light direct administration backed by occasional military deployment.

sources.label: Felix Padel, The Sacrifice of Human Being: British Rule and the Konds of Orissa (1995)
John Campbell, A Personal Narrative of Thirteen Years' Service amongst the Wild Tribes of Khondistan (1864)
